guide.label: Flashing red
guide.text: Stop completely, then go when safe, as if at a stop sign.

meta.sourceSection: Section 4A.04, meanings of flashing signal indications.

content.question: Ahead of you, the traffic light over an intersection is flashing yellow for your direction. What should you do?

choices.text: Slow down and go through with care, yielding as needed
Stop completely, then go when the way is clear
Speed up to clear the intersection before it turns red
Stop and wait, since the light is about to turn red

content.explanation: A flashing yellow light lets you go on without stopping, with caution. Slow down and yield to anyone already in the intersection or the crosswalk.

guide.label: Flashing yellow
guide.text: Slow down and go with caution, yielding to anyone already in the intersection.

meta.sourceSection: Section 1.5, Signs, Signals and Road Markings, under Crosswalk Lines.

content.question: You are riding along a residential block when you see crosswalk lines painted across the road, well away from any intersection. A pedestrian is crossing in them. Who has the right-of-way?

choices.text: The pedestrian, just as at a corner crosswalk
You do, since crosswalks count only at corners
You do, since no signal controls the crossing
Whoever reaches the crosswalk first

content.explanation: Pedestrians in a crosswalk have the right-of-way over vehicles, and a crosswalk can sit in the middle of a block as well as at a corner.

guide.text: Pedestrians in a crosswalk have the right-of-way, including at a crosswalk in the middle of a block.

meta.sourceSection: Section 1.5, Signs, Signals and Road Markings, under Turn Lanes.

content.question: In Georgia, a center lane bordered by yellow lines is marked for left turns. What may you use it for?

choices.text: Making a left turn, and nothing else
Passing a slower vehicle when the way is clear
Riding past a line of stopped traffic
Pulling out of traffic if your motorcycle breaks down

content.explanation: Georgia law reserves the center turn lane for left turns and allows no other use of it.

guide.label: Center left-turn lane
guide.text: For left turns only, never for passing or travel.

meta.sourceSection: Section 1.5, Signs, Signals and Road Markings, under Turn Lanes.

content.question: In Georgia, how far ahead of your left turn may you move into a center left-turn lane?

choices.text: No more than 300 feet before the turn
No more than 100 feet before the turn
No more than 500 feet before the turn
Any distance, as long as you signal first

content.explanation: You may enter the center turn lane no more than 300 feet before your left turn. Watch for a driver coming the other way who moves into the same lane to turn.

guide.label: Entering the center turn lane
guide.text: Enter no more than 300 feet before your turn. Watch for oncoming drivers using it too.

meta.sourceSection: Section 1.5, Signs, Signals and Road Markings, under Bicycle Lanes.

content.question: In Georgia, when may you ride your motorcycle in a marked bicycle lane?

choices.text: Only to cross it to make a turn
Whenever no cyclists are in it
To get around traffic stopped beside it
To park, if you leave cyclists room

content.explanation: Georgia bars motor vehicles from driving or parking in a bicycle lane. You may cross one only to make a turn, and you yield to any cyclist in it as you do.

guide.text: Never ride or park in a bicycle lane. Cross it only to turn, yielding to cyclists.

meta.sourceSection: Section 7, Signs, Signals and Markings, Roundabouts, the multilane panel.

content.question: You are coming up to a roundabout with two lanes. When should you pick the lane you will use?

choices.text: Before you enter, then keep to it until you leave
Once inside, moving over as your exit comes up
Any time inside, as long as you signal first
At your exit, crossing to the outer lane to leave

content.explanation: Follow the lane signs and pavement arrows to get into the right lane before you enter. Once in the roundabout, keep to that lane until you leave.

guide.text: In a multilane roundabout, choose your lane before entering and never change lanes inside.

meta.sourceSection: Section 7, Signs, Signals and Markings, Roundabouts, the motorist panels.

content.question: You are circling a roundabout and the road you want is the next exit. How do you leave?

choices.text: Signal, then bear right onto your exit
Bear right with no signal, since all exits go right
Stop in the circle until the exit road is clear
Move to the outside lane first, then turn off

content.explanation: Traffic in a roundabout circulates counterclockwise, and you leave it by signaling, then bearing right. Watch for pedestrians in the crosswalk as you exit.

guide.text: Traffic circles counterclockwise. To leave, signal, then bear right, watching for pedestrians.

meta.sourceSection: Section 1.5, Signs, Signals and Road Markings, opening paragraph.

content.question: A police officer directing traffic at an intersection waves you through, but the light facing you is red. What should you do?

choices.text: Go, following the officer's direction
Stay stopped until the light turns green
Treat the red as a stop sign, then go when clear
Go only if no one waits on the cross street

content.explanation: You obey signs and signals unless a police officer or emergency worker directs you otherwise, and then the officer's direction comes first.

guide.text: A police officer's or emergency worker's directions override signs and signals.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under Laws Governing Right-of-Way.

content.question: You have the right-of-way at an intersection, but a driver on the cross street starts to pull out as if they have not seen you. What should you do?

choices.text: Give way to avoid a crash, though the turn was yours
Hold your line, since the law gives you the right-of-way
Sound your horn and keep going so the driver stops
Speed up to get through before the driver reaches you

content.explanation: The law says who should go first, but it never entitles you to force the point. When a driver moves into your path anyway, giving way is how you avoid the crash.

guide.text: Right-of-way is given, never taken. Yield even when it is yours if that prevents a crash.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under Laws Governing Right-of-Way.

content.question: You and a car reach an intersection with no signs or signals at the same moment. The car is on your right. Who must yield?

choices.text: You must, since the car is on your right
The car must, since you are on its left
Whichever of you is going faster
The car, since a motorcycle is harder to see

content.explanation: At an intersection with no signs or signals, when two vehicles arrive together, the one on the left yields to the one on the right.

guide.text: No signs or signals and two arrive together: the vehicle on the left yields to the one on the right.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under Laws Governing Right-of-Way.

content.question: At an intersection with a stop sign on every corner, in what order do vehicles go?

choices.text: First to stop, first to go, after pedestrians cross
Traffic on the wider road goes first
Straight traffic first, then turning traffic
Vehicles on the left before those on the right

content.explanation: At an all-way stop, pedestrians go first, then vehicles go in the order they arrived. If two arrive at about the same time, yield to the one on your right.

guide.text: All-way stop: pedestrians first, then first to arrive, first to go. A tie yields to the vehicle on the right.

meta.sourceSection: Section 4A.03, meanings of steady signal indications.

content.question: You are turning left on a green light, and an oncoming car is close to the intersection. Who has the right-of-way?

choices.text: The oncoming car, so you wait for it to pass
You do, since your light is green
You do, since you reached the intersection first
You do, if your turn signal came on first

content.explanation: A green light lets you turn left, but not ahead of oncoming traffic close enough to be a hazard. Yield to it, and to anyone already in the intersection or crosswalk.

guide.label: Green light, turning left
guide.text: Yield to oncoming traffic close enough to be a hazard.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Laws Governing Right-of-Way; Section 9, Exiting and Entering Driveways.

content.question: You are riding out of a parking garage, across a sidewalk, to enter a street. What must you do?

choices.text: Stop before the sidewalk, then yield to anyone in your way
Roll slowly across the sidewalk, then stop at the street
Stop only at the street's edge, yielding to vehicles
Go once the street is clear, since walkers will see you

content.explanation: Coming out of a driveway, alley or garage, stop before the sidewalk and go on only once pedestrians are clear. Then yield to every vehicle already on the road you are entering.

guide.text: Entering or leaving a driveway or alley, stop for pedestrians on the sidewalk. Coming out, yield to all traffic on the road.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under Laws Governing Right-of-Way.

content.question: An ambulance with its siren on and lights flashing is coming up behind you. What should you do?

choices.text: Slow down, pull to the right edge of the road and stop
Speed up to stay ahead of it until you can turn off
Stop at once in your lane so it can go around you
Move into the left lane so it can pass on your right

content.explanation: Slow down and move onto the shoulder, or as far right as you can, and stop. Never stop where you would block an intersection or a turn the emergency vehicle needs.

guide.text: For an emergency vehicle using lights and siren, slow down, pull to the right and stop, clear of any intersection.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, Highway Work Zones, under Yield to Amber Lights.

content.question: You come up behind a slow road-maintenance truck with flashing amber lights in a work zone. What must you do?

choices.text: Slow down and yield the right-of-way to it
Pass it quickly, since it is moving so slowly
Follow it closely so other traffic cannot cut in
Sound your horn so its driver pulls aside

content.explanation: In a work zone, maintenance vehicles and workers have the right-of-way. Slow down for amber-lit work vehicles, give way to them, and follow any arrows or signs they show.

guide.text: In a work zone, yield to workers and to work vehicles showing amber lights.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, the Move Over Law box.

content.question: In Georgia, a police car with flashing lights is stopped on the shoulder ahead, and traffic in the next lane keeps you from moving over. What must you do?

choices.text: Slow below the speed limit and be ready to stop
Keep your speed but ride at the far side of your lane
Stop in your lane until the next lane clears
Nothing more, as long as you are within the limit

content.explanation: Georgia's Move Over law says to move a lane away from a stopped emergency, sanitation or utility vehicle on the shoulder. When you cannot, slow below the speed limit and be ready to stop.

guide.label: Move Over law
guide.text: Move a lane away from a stopped emergency, sanitation or utility vehicle. If you can't, slow below the limit.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, Passing, under Passing Stopped Cars.

content.question: A car in the lane next to yours has stopped at a crosswalk to let a pedestrian cross. May you ride past it?

choices.text: No, not while it is stopped there
Yes, if the pedestrian is not yet in your lane
Yes, if you slow down and sound your horn
Yes, since it is in a different lane from yours

content.explanation: When a vehicle stops for someone at a crosswalk, no one coming up from behind may pass it, in any lane. It can hide a pedestrian who is about to step into your path.

guide.text: Never pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk for a pedestrian, even from the next lane.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, Highway Work Zones, under Obey Flaggers.

content.question: A flagger in a work zone signals you to stop, though there is no stop sign or signal there. What should you do?

choices.text: Stop, since the flagger's direction binds you like a sign
Slow down, then go on if the way looks clear
Go on, since only a sign or signal can require a stop
Stop only if a police officer stands with the flagger

content.explanation: A work-zone flagger carries the authority of a regulatory sign, so obey a flagger's directions as you would the sign itself.

guide.text: A work-zone flagger has the authority of a regulatory sign.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under Laws Governing Right-of-Way.

content.question: You reach a red light where you want to turn right, and no sign forbids turning on red. What may you do?

choices.text: Stop fully, then turn once traffic and pedestrians clear
Slow down, then turn without stopping if the way is clear
Wait for the green, since a red light means stay stopped
Turn on red only where a sign says it is allowed

content.explanation: A red light still allows a right turn unless a sign says otherwise. Stop completely, and turn only once traffic and pedestrians have gone by and the turn is safe.

guide.label: Right turn on red
guide.text: Allowed after a full stop and yielding, unless a sign forbids it.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under Laws Governing Right-of-Way.

content.question: After a full stop at a red light, where are you allowed to turn left?

choices.text: From a one-way street onto a one-way street going left
From a one-way street onto a two-way cross street
From a two-way street, once oncoming traffic has cleared
Nowhere, since turning on red applies to right turns

content.explanation: Turning left on red is allowed only from one one-way street onto another that carries traffic to your left. Turn from the left lane, after a full stop, once traffic and pedestrians are clear, and never where a sign forbids it.

guide.label: Left turn on red
guide.text: Only from a one-way street onto a one-way street flowing to your left, after a full stop.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under Laws Governing Right-of-Way.

content.question: A school bus ahead of you switches on its flashing yellow lights. What does that tell you?

choices.text: It is about to stop, so slow down and be ready to stop
It has stopped to unload, so you must stop right away
It is pulling away, so you may pass it with care
It is turning soon, so you may pass it on the left

content.explanation: Yellow lights flashing on a school bus mean it is getting ready to stop for children. Slow down so you can stop when it does, and look out for children on or beside the road.

guide.text: Flashing yellow lights on a school bus mean it is about to stop. Slow down and get ready to stop.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Laws Governing Right-of-Way; Section 9, Sharing the Road With School Buses.

content.question: A school bus has stopped ahead with red lights flashing and its stop arm out, and you have stopped behind it. When may you go on?

choices.text: When it moves or its lights go off, and children are clear
As soon as the children you can see are off the road
Once you have stopped fully and no children are in sight
When the bus driver signals you to go around it

content.explanation: With red lights flashing and the stop arm out, no one may pass the bus. Stay stopped until two things are true: the bus has moved off or turned its signals off, and the children are clear of the road.

guide.text: Red lights and stop arm out: stop, and stay stopped until the bus moves or its signals go off and children are clear.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Laws Governing Right-of-Way; Section 9, Sharing the Road With School Buses.

content.question: On a highway divided by a median, a school bus on the other side of the median stops with its red lights flashing. What must you do?

choices.text: Keep going with care, watching for children
Stop until the bus moves or turns its lights off
Stop, then go on once no children are in sight
Slow to 25 mph until you have passed the bus

content.explanation: A median changes the rule. Only traffic going the same way as the bus has to stop, so you may keep going, while watching for any child near the road.

guide.text: Where a median divides the highway, only traffic going the bus's direction must stop for it.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under How To Make A Right Turn.

content.question: You turn right from a one-lane street onto a street with two lanes going your way. Which lane should you end up in?

choices.text: The right lane of the street you turn onto
The left lane, to stay clear of parked cars
Whichever lane has the least traffic in it
The left lane, if you will turn left soon

content.explanation: A right turn ends in the right lane of the street you turn onto, without entering any other lane. Where several lanes turn right together, finish in the lane matching the one you turned from.

guide.text: Finish a right turn in the right lane of the street you enter. With several turning lanes, keep to your matching lane.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under How To Make A Left Turn.

content.question: You are turning left onto a four-lane street, two lanes each way. Which lane should you turn into?

choices.text: The lane next to the center line on your side
The lane nearest the curb, to leave room for traffic
Whichever lane is clear when you start the turn
The curb lane, then move over once you are straight

content.explanation: Start a left turn from the far left lane or the turn lane, and finish it in the lane nearest the center of the road. Lane changes inside the intersection are not allowed.

guide.text: Turn left from the far left lane or turn lane into the lane nearest the center. Never change lanes mid-intersection.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under U-Turns.

content.question: Where is a U-turn against the law even when no sign forbids it?

choices.text: On a curve where approaching drivers cannot see you
At an intersection controlled by a traffic signal
On a road with a speed limit of 45 mph or more
On a road with one lane in each direction

content.explanation: A U-turn is illegal wherever drivers coming from either direction cannot see you, such as on a curve or close to the crest of a hill. It is also illegal where a sign prohibits it.

guide.text: No U-turn on a curve or near a hilltop where other drivers can't see you, or where a sign forbids it.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under Stopping, Standing, and Parking.

content.question: Your motorcycle breaks down on a highway. Where should you try to leave it?

choices.text: Off the road, where drivers can see it from 200 feet each way
Off the road, where drivers can see it from 50 feet each way
On the edge of the travel lane, with your hazard lights on
Just past a curve, where it is out of the way of traffic

content.explanation: You may not park on the highway itself. If your motorcycle breaks down, get it off the road if you possibly can, somewhere traffic can pass freely and drivers can see it from 200 feet away in either direction.

guide.label: Broken-down vehicle
guide.text: Move it off the road, where it is visible for 200 feet both ways.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under Stopping, Standing, and Parking.

content.question: You want to stop for a moment to let your passenger off. Which of these places is off limits for that?

choices.text: On a crosswalk
In front of a driveway
Within 15 feet of a fire hydrant
Within 30 feet of a stop sign

content.explanation: Some places allow a quick stop to pick up or drop off a passenger, such as near a hydrant, a stop sign or a driveway. A crosswalk is never one of them: no stopping, standing or parking there at any time.

guide.text: Never stop, even for a moment, on a crosswalk or sidewalk, in an intersection, or on railroad tracks.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under Stopping, Standing, and Parking.

content.question: How close to a fire hydrant may you park?

choices.text: No closer than 15 feet
No closer than 5 feet
No closer than 30 feet
No closer than 50 feet

content.explanation: Park at least 15 feet from a fire hydrant. Closer than that, you may stop only for a moment to pick up or drop off a passenger.

guide.label: Fire hydrant
guide.text: Park at least 15 feet away.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under Following Emergency Vehicles.

content.question: A fire truck answering an alarm passes you, and you end up riding behind it. How closely may you follow it?

choices.text: No closer than 200 feet
No closer than 100 feet
No closer than 500 feet
No closer than 50 feet

content.explanation: Stay at least 200 feet behind a fire truck responding to an alarm. Once it stops at a fire, do not park within 500 feet of it.

guide.label: Fire truck on an alarm
guide.text: Follow no closer than 200 feet.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, Passing, under Weaving.

content.question: Traffic on a multi-lane highway is moving slower than you would like. May you weave from lane to lane to get ahead?

choices.text: No, weaving to beat the flow of traffic is unlawful
Yes, as long as you signal every lane change
Yes, as long as you stay under the speed limit
Yes, since a motorcycle needs less room than a car

content.explanation: Georgia law doesn't let you dart between lanes to get ahead of the traffic around you. Change lanes only when it is safe, and signal clearly each time.

guide.text: Weaving from lane to lane to get ahead of traffic is illegal.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Turn Signals and Making Turns Safely, under Illegal Signals.

content.question: A driver behind you wants to pass. May you flash your turn signal to tell them it is safe to go around?

choices.text: No, a turn signal used as a go-ahead is illegal
Yes, it is the usual courtesy signal to pass
Yes, if you flash the left signal, not the right
Yes, but only where passing is allowed

content.explanation: A turn signal can't legally be used as a go-ahead in Georgia, so never flash one to tell the driver behind you it is safe to pass.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, the Keep Right Except to Pass box.

content.question: You are riding at the speed limit in the left lane of a road with two lanes your way, and a faster vehicle comes up behind you. What must you do?

choices.text: Move to the right and let it go by
Hold your lane, since you are at the limit
Speed up until it no longer has to wait
Slow down so it can pass you on the right

content.explanation: The left lane is for passing. When faster traffic comes up behind you there, move right whatever speed you are doing, unless traffic, weather, a hazard or a left exit or turn keeps you in that lane.

guide.text: Leave the passing lane for faster traffic behind you, even when you are at the speed limit.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under Driving Too Slowly.

content.question: A highway has a posted minimum speed that your small motorcycle cannot keep up with. What should you do?

choices.text: Take a different route
Ride on the shoulder with your flashers on
Keep to the right lane at your best speed
Ride it only when traffic is light

content.explanation: Riding so slowly that you hold up normal traffic is against the law, unless a lower speed is needed for safety. If you cannot reach a highway's posted minimum, use another route.

guide.text: Never ride so slowly that you hold up traffic. If you can't reach a posted minimum speed, use another route.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under Speed Limits.

content.question: In Georgia, what is the speed limit in a residential district when no limit is posted?

choices.text: 30 mph
25 mph
35 mph
45 mph

content.explanation: Unless a sign says otherwise, Georgia's limit in any urban or residential district is 30 mph.

guide.label: Urban or residential district
guide.text: 30 mph unless posted otherwise.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under Speed Limits.

content.question: In Georgia, what is the speed limit on a rural interstate when no other limit is posted?

choices.text: 70 mph
65 mph
55 mph
75 mph

content.explanation: Georgia's limit on a rural interstate is 70 mph unless posted otherwise. On an urban interstate it drops to 65.

guide.label: Rural interstate
guide.text: 70 mph unless posted otherwise.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under Coasting.

content.question: You are riding down a long hill. May you shift into neutral and coast to the bottom?

choices.text: No, coasting downhill in neutral is illegal
Yes, if you keep a hand ready on the front brake
Yes, to save fuel on a long, gentle grade
Yes, as long as you stay under the speed limit

content.explanation: Traveling downhill with the transmission in neutral is against the law. Stay in gear on the way down.

guide.text: Coasting downhill with the transmission in neutral is illegal.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under Aggressive Driving.

content.question: Which of these counts as aggressive driving under the law?

choices.text: Tailgating a driver to pressure them to move over
Passing a slow car where passing is allowed
Riding at the speed limit in the right lane
Using your horn to warn a driver drifting toward you

content.explanation: Driving in a way meant to harass, frighten or block another person is aggressive driving. Cutting someone off, riding on their tail, or refusing to let them pass or change lanes are all examples.

guide.text: Aggressive driving is driving meant to harass, frighten or block someone, such as tailgating or cutting them off.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under Impaired Hearing and Vision.

content.question: In Georgia, when is it illegal to wear headphones or a headset while you ride?

choices.text: When they keep you from hearing what is around you
When they are wired to a phone rather than wireless
When they are not built into your helmet
When they play music rather than a phone call

content.explanation: In Georgia, riding with headphones or a headset that impairs your hearing is against the law, and unsafe besides.

guide.text: Riding with headphones or a headset that impairs your hearing is illegal.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, Texting and Cell Phone Use While Driving.

content.question: Georgia's Hands-Free law applies while you ride. Which of these does it forbid?

choices.text: Holding your phone in one hand to take a call
Taking a call on a phone fixed in a handlebar mount
Carrying your phone in a bag strapped to the seat
Leaving your phone switched on while you ride

content.explanation: Georgia's Hands-Free law bars holding or supporting a phone with any part of your body while you ride. A mounted phone or a wireless device may be used, but writing, sending or reading texts, and watching or recording video, stay off limits.

guide.text: Never hold or support a phone with your body while riding, and never text or watch video, even on a mounted phone.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, Passing, under How To Pass On A Two-Lane Road.

content.question: In Georgia, you are passing on a two-lane road. You must be back in your own lane before an oncoming vehicle comes within what distance?

choices.text: 200 feet
100 feet
50 feet
500 feet

content.explanation: In Georgia, a pass has to be finished, with you fully back in the right lane, before oncoming traffic is within 200 feet. It also has to end before the passing zone does and before you reach an intersection.

guide.label: Finishing a pass
guide.text: Back in your lane before oncoming traffic is within 200 feet, the passing zone ends, or an intersection.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, Passing, under Passing is prohibited on two-lane roads.

content.question: In Georgia, on a two-lane road, passing is banned within how many feet of a railroad crossing, bridge or tunnel?

choices.text: 100 feet
50 feet
200 feet
500 feet

content.explanation: Georgia bars passing on a two-lane road within 100 feet of a railroad crossing, or of a bridge, viaduct or tunnel.

guide.label: No passing near
guide.text: A railroad crossing, bridge, viaduct or tunnel: not within 100 feet, on a two-lane road.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, Passing, under Passing is prohibited on two-lane roads.

content.question: Which of these is a place where passing is not allowed?

choices.text: On a hill where you can't see oncoming traffic
Where a broken yellow line is on your side
Around an obstruction, after yielding to oncoming traffic
On a road with two marked lanes going your way

content.explanation: Never pass on a hill or a curve where you cannot see oncoming vehicles close enough to be a danger. Passing on the shoulder is barred too.

guide.text: No passing on a hill or curve where you can't see oncoming traffic, or on the shoulder.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, Passing, under Passing On The Right.

content.question: On a road with one lane each way, when may you pass another vehicle on its right?

choices.text: When it is turning left and the road is wide enough
When it is going slower than the speed limit
When the shoulder is wide enough to ride on
When its driver waves you around on the right

content.explanation: You may pass on the right of a vehicle that is turning left, as long as the pavement is wide enough for both of you. On a road with two or more lanes your way, passing on the right is allowed too. The shoulder is never used for it.

guide.text: Pass on the right only around a left-turning vehicle with room to spare, or where two or more lanes go your way.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, Passing, under When Someone Passes You.

content.question: A car is passing you. Which of these is against the law?

choices.text: Speeding up before it has finished passing you
Easing off the throttle a little to let it by
Keeping your speed steady as it goes by
Covering your brake while it goes by

content.explanation: Let a vehicle that is passing you get completely by before you speed up again; picking up speed while it passes is illegal. Easing off slightly to help it past is a courtesy.

guide.text: Never speed up while someone is passing you. Easing off slightly is a courtesy.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, Passing, under Passing Bicycles.

content.question: In Georgia, you are passing a bicycle and cannot move to a lane away from it. How much space must you leave?

choices.text: At least 3 feet
At least 2 feet
At least 5 feet
At least 10 feet

content.explanation: In Georgia, move into a lane not next to the bicycle if you can. If you can't, slow to 10 mph under the limit or to 25 mph, whichever is faster, and keep at least 3 feet between you and the rider.

guide.label: Passing a bicycle
guide.text: A lane away if you can. If not, slow down and leave at least 3 feet.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, Passing, under Passing Motorcyclists.

content.question: A car behind you wants to pass. May it pass you while staying in your lane?

choices.text: No, it must pass you using the next lane
Yes, if you are riding at one side of the lane
Yes, if it leaves you at least 3 feet
Yes, in slow traffic where it can't change lanes

content.explanation: A motorcyclist is legally entitled to the full width of a lane. A driver passing you has to do it from the next lane, never from inside yours.

guide.text: A motorcycle is entitled to a full lane. No one may pass you inside it.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5.4, Space Management, under Lane Sharing.

content.question: In Georgia, traffic ahead is stopped in both lanes. Should you ride between the rows of cars to reach the front?

choices.text: No, stay in a lane of your own
Yes, if you keep your speed low and steady
Yes, as long as the cars are fully stopped
Yes, if there is room for your mirrors to clear

content.explanation: Georgia's manual tells riders not to share a lane with other vehicles or ride between rows of stopped or moving traffic. A motorcycle needs a full lane as much as a car does, and squeezing between cars leaves you exposed, with almost no space around you.

guide.text: Don't share a lane with other vehicles or ride between rows of stopped or moving traffic.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, Highway Work Zones, under Adjust Your Lane Position.

content.question: In a work zone, crews are working right beside your lane and the next lane is closed. Where should you ride?

choices.text: Within your lane, on the side away from the workers
In the center of your lane, as you normally would
On the side nearest them, so traffic can pass you
In the center, faster, to get past them sooner

content.explanation: Where workers are close to your lane, shift away from them within it. The extra distance protects them and you.

guide.text: Riding past workers close to your lane, shift away from them within it.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under Railroad Crossings.

content.question: In Georgia, the signals are flashing at a railroad crossing ahead. Where must you stop?

choices.text: Between 15 and 50 feet from the nearest rail
Between 5 and 15 feet from the nearest rail
Between 50 and 100 feet from the nearest rail
Anywhere, as long as you are off the tracks

content.explanation: When a crossing's signals flash, its gates are down, a flagger signals or a train is close, stop no nearer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the nearest rail.

guide.label: Stopping at a railroad crossing
guide.text: Between 15 and 50 feet from the nearest rail.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under Railroad Crossings.

content.question: The gates at a railroad crossing are down, but you can't see a train coming. What should you do?

choices.text: Stay stopped until the gates go up and the tracks are clear
Ride around the gates with care, since no train is coming
Ride under the gate arm, since a motorcycle fits
Cross once the lights stop flashing, gates or not

content.explanation: Never ride around or under a lowered railroad crossing gate. Stay stopped until every track is clear, the signals have stopped flashing and the gates are up.

guide.text: Never go around or under a lowered railroad crossing gate. Wait until the gates rise and every track is clear.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5.7, Speed Management, under Railroad Crossings.

content.question: You are about to cross railroad tracks, and traffic is backed up just past the far rail. What should you do?

choices.text: Wait until there is room to clear the crossing completely
Start across and stop just past the last rail
Start across, since the traffic will move up soon
Squeeze past the stopped cars on the far side

content.explanation: Look both ways, and start across only when you are sure you can clear the whole crossing without stopping. A train sticks out about three feet past the rails on each side.

guide.text: Cross tracks only when you can clear the whole crossing without stopping. A train is wider than the rails.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5.7, Speed Management, under Railroad Crossings.

content.question: Your motorcycle stalls on railroad tracks, and a train is coming. What should you do?

choices.text: Get off and move away, toward the side the train comes from
Get off and run the same way the train is heading
Keep trying to restart it until the train is close
Push it clear of the tracks before you move away

content.explanation: Get off at once and move quickly away from the tracks, toward the direction the train is coming from. Run the way it is heading and you could be hit by debris when it strikes the motorcycle. Then call for help.

guide.text: Stalled on the tracks with a train coming: get off and move away, toward the side the train comes from, so debris flies past you.

meta.sourceSection: Section 1.5, round sign caption; Section 5.7, under Railroad Crossings.

content.question: A train is approaching a crossing ahead, and you think you can get across before it arrives. What should you do?

choices.text: Stop and let the train go by
Speed up and cross before it reaches you
Cross only if the gates have not come down yet
Sound your horn and cross quickly

content.explanation: Never try to beat a train to a crossing. It is nearer and moving faster than it looks, and it cannot stop in time for you.

guide.text: Never try to beat a train. It is nearer and faster than it looks, and it can't stop for you.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2.4, Georgia's Impaired Driving Laws and Penalties.

content.question: In Georgia, at what blood alcohol concentration is a rider legally under the influence?

choices.text: 0.08 at 21 or older, 0.02 under 21
0.08 at 21 or older, 0.05 under 21
0.10 at 21 or older, 0.02 under 21
0.08 for every rider, whatever their age

content.explanation: In Georgia, a rider 21 or older is under the influence at a BAC of 0.08 or more, and a rider under 21 at 0.02. Impairment begins well below either.

guide.label: Legal BAC limit
guide.text: 0.08 at 21 or older, 0.02 under 21.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under Driving Under the Influence of Drugs or Alcohol.

content.question: A medicine your doctor prescribed leaves you drowsy, and you ride anyway. Is the prescription a defense to a DUI charge?

choices.text: No, not if the medicine impairs your riding
Yes, prescribed medicine is lawful to ride on
Yes, if you took no more than the prescribed dose
Yes, unless you also had something to drink

content.explanation: A prescription is no defense if the medicine impairs your ability to ride safely. A drug can leave you legally under the influence whether it was prescribed or not.

guide.text: A prescription is no defense to DUI if the medicine impairs your riding.

meta.sourceSection: Section 10, Losing Your Driving Privileges, under Implied Consent.

content.question: An officer asks you to take a state chemical test for alcohol or drugs. Which is true?

choices.text: The law requires it, and you may then get your own test too
You may refuse it with no effect on your license
You may take a test of your own choosing in its place
You need take it only if you failed a roadside check

content.explanation: The law requires you to submit to the state's chemical tests of your blood, breath, urine or other bodily substances. Once you have, you may have more tests done by someone you choose, at your own cost.

guide.text: You must take the state's chemical test when an officer asks. Afterward you may get your own, at your cost.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under Use Headlights Properly.

content.question: In Georgia, you are riding at night with your high beam on. You must switch to low beam when an oncoming vehicle comes within what distance?

choices.text: 500 feet
200 feet
1,000 feet
100 feet

content.explanation: Dim to low beam within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle, and within 200 feet of a vehicle you are following, so your light does not blind its driver.

guide.label: Dim your high beam
guide.text: Within 500 feet of oncoming traffic, and 200 feet behind a vehicle.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5, Traffic Laws, under Night Driving.

content.question: On a dark road at night, what should decide how fast you ride?

choices.text: Being able to stop within the reach of your headlight
Keeping up with the speed of the traffic around you
The posted speed limit, and nothing else
How far ahead you can see other vehicles' lights

content.explanation: Never ride so fast that you could not stop within the distance your headlight lights up.

meta.sourceSection: Section 8, Safety Guidelines, under Fog.

content.question: You have to ride through heavy fog. Should you turn on your hazard flashers?

choices.text: No, ride with your low beam and no flashers
Yes, so drivers behind you can see you
Yes, but only while you are on a highway
Yes, whenever you have to slow down

content.explanation: Don't ride in fog with your parking lights or hazard flashers on. Use your low beam, slow down, and slow further when lights appear ahead, since distance is hard to judge in fog.

guide.text: In fog, keep hazard flashers and parking lights off. Use your low beam and slow down.

meta.sourceSection: Section 11, Crashes, under Deer-Automobile Crashes.

content.question: A deer runs across the road ahead of you and into the trees. What should you expect next?

choices.text: Another deer may be following close behind
The road is clear, since deer usually travel alone
The road is clear, since the deer was scared off
The deer will now keep well away from the road

content.explanation: Slow down whenever a deer crosses ahead. Deer usually move in groups, so another is likely close behind. Watch for them most in the early morning and late evening.

guide.text: When one deer crosses ahead, slow down and expect another close behind.

meta.sourceSection: Section 8, Safety Guidelines, under Entering Expressways.

content.question: You are joining an expressway from an entrance ramp. What should you do in the acceleration lane?

choices.text: Match the speed of expressway traffic, then merge when safe
Keep to ramp speed so traffic can pass before you merge
Merge at once, since expressway traffic must make room
Hold back until a driver on the expressway waves you in

content.explanation: Use the acceleration lane to bring your speed up to that of expressway traffic, then merge when it is safe. Traffic already on the expressway has the right-of-way.

guide.text: Joining an expressway, match traffic's speed in the acceleration lane and merge when safe. Traffic already on it has the right-of-way.

meta.sourceSection: Section 8, Safety Guidelines, under Gores.

content.question: Joining an expressway, a solid white line separates your acceleration lane from the travel lane beside it. What does the law require?

choices.text: Stay in the acceleration lane until the solid line ends
Cross the line as soon as you see a gap in traffic
Cross the line once you have signaled your merge
Cross it with care, as you would a dashed lane line

content.explanation: The solid white line between an acceleration lane and the travel lane marks off the gore, and crossing it is against the law. Stay in the acceleration lane until the line ends, then merge.

guide.text: Entering an expressway, never cross the solid white line beside the acceleration lane. Merge after it ends.

meta.sourceSection: Section 6.3, Sharing the Road.

content.question: You are riding alone on an expressway that has an HOV lane marked with a diamond. May you use it?

choices.text: Yes, a motorcycle may use it with only its rider aboard
No, not unless you are carrying a passenger
No, not during the hours its limits are posted
No, not unless you have a toll account

content.explanation: Motorcycles may use HOV lanes however many people are riding, a rider alone included.

meta.sourceSection: Section 8, Safety Guidelines, under Tips For Expressway Driving.

content.question: On an expressway, which of these is a reason you may stop on the shoulder?

choices.text: Your motorcycle has broken down
You need to stretch after a long ride
You want to get something from your saddlebag
You and your passenger want to swap seats

content.explanation: Stopping on an expressway shoulder is dangerous and allowed only in an emergency. Stretching, fetching something or changing riders is not an emergency, so use a rest area.

guide.text: Stop on an expressway shoulder only in an emergency, never to stretch, swap riders or fetch something.

meta.sourceSection: Section 8, Safety Guidelines, under Tips For Expressway Driving.

content.question: An oncoming car has its left turn signal flashing. What does that tell you for certain?

choices.text: Nothing for certain, since the driver may not turn
The driver will turn left at the next chance
The driver has seen you and will wait for you
The driver will slow down before turning

content.explanation: Never count on other drivers to do what you expect. A flashing left signal does not mean the driver is going to turn left, so keep an escape route in mind.

guide.text: A flashing turn signal doesn't prove the driver will turn. Don't count on it.

meta.sourceSection: Section 9, Sharing the Road, under Georgia's Law Concerning Pedestrians.

content.question: At a crosswalk with no signal, on a road with two lanes each way, a pedestrian is crossing in the oncoming lane nearest the center line. What must you do?

choices.text: Stop and stay stopped to let them cross
Keep going, since they are not on your side yet
Slow down, then go if they are not in your lane
Sound your horn so they wait for you to pass

content.explanation: Stop and stay stopped for a pedestrian in a crosswalk who is on your half of the road, or within one lane of it. Your half means every lane carrying traffic your way.

guide.text: At a crosswalk, stop for a pedestrian on your half of the road or within one lane of it.

meta.sourceSection: Section 9, Sharing the Road, under Blind Pedestrians.

content.question: A person using a white cane starts across the street ahead of you, away from any crosswalk. What should you do?

choices.text: Stop and give them the right-of-way
Go ahead, since they are not in a crosswalk
Sound your horn to warn them you are coming
Ride slowly around them on the far side

content.explanation: A pedestrian using a white cane or a guide dog has the right-of-way at all times, crosswalk or not.

meta.sourceSection: Section 9, Sharing the Road, under Crosswalks.

content.question: An intersection has no painted crosswalk lines. Is there a crosswalk there?

choices.text: Yes, every corner of an intersection has one
No, a crosswalk exists only where it is painted
Only where a pedestrian signal is posted
Only if a school or park is nearby

content.explanation: Crosswalks exist at all four corners of an intersection, painted or not, where the sidewalk would carry across the street. Between intersections, a crosswalk exists only where it is marked.

guide.text: Every corner of an intersection has a crosswalk, painted or not.

meta.sourceSection: Section 9, Sharing the Road, under Passing Stopped Cars in Lanes of Travel.

content.question: In Georgia, on a road with two lanes your way, you stop to let a pedestrian use a crosswalk. Where should you stop?

choices.text: At least 10 feet before the crosswalk
Right at the edge of the crosswalk
At least 3 feet before the crosswalk
At least 30 feet before the crosswalk

content.explanation: Stopping at least 10 feet short of the crosswalk lets a driver in the next lane see the pedestrian you stopped for.

guide.label: Stopping for a crosswalk, multi-lane road
guide.text: At least 10 feet back, so the next lane can see the pedestrian.

meta.sourceSection: Section 9, Sharing the Road, under Sharing the Road With Bicycles.

content.question: A bicyclist is riding in the travel lane even though a bike lane runs beside it. Which is true?

choices.text: The rider may use the full lane and need not use the bike lane
The rider must move into the bike lane when there is one
You may pass in the same lane, since bicycles keep right
You may sound your horn to move the rider over

content.explanation: Bicyclists may ride on every road but limited-access highways, may use the full lane, and need not ride in a bike lane even where there is one. Yield to them as you would to any other road user.

guide.text: Cyclists may use the full lane and need not ride in a bike lane. Yield to them as to any vehicle.

meta.sourceSection: Section 6.3, Sharing the Road.

content.question: A fully loaded tractor-trailer is traveling at 55 mph. About how much distance does it need to stop, compared with a car?

choices.text: About three times as much
About the same
About twice as much
About ten times as much

content.explanation: A fully loaded tractor-trailer at 55 mph needs about three times a car's distance to stop. Ride with extra caution near one.

guide.label: Loaded truck at 55 mph
guide.text: Needs about three times a car's distance to stop.

meta.sourceSection: Section 6.3, Sharing the Road.

content.question: You are riding near a large truck. How can you tell whether its driver can see you?

choices.text: If you can't see the driver in its side mirror, they can't see you
If you can see its side mirrors, the driver can see you too
If your headlight is on, the driver is sure to see you
If you stay close behind it, the driver sees you in a mirror

content.explanation: A truck has large blind spots directly ahead, directly behind and along both sides, worst on the right. If you can't see the driver's reflection in the side mirror, the driver can't see you, so don't stay there any longer than it takes to pass.

guide.text: Near a truck, if you can't see the driver in its side mirror, the driver can't see you. Don't linger there.

meta.sourceSection: Section 11, Crashes, under If You Are Involved In A Crash.

content.question: In Georgia, you are involved in a crash. When must you notify the police right away?

choices.text: When anyone is hurt, or damage tops $500
When someone is hurt, but not for damage alone
When damage tops $1,500, or someone is hurt
When the other driver asks you to call them

content.explanation: In Georgia, after a crash, stop in a safe place and notify the nearest police agency at once if anyone is hurt, or if property damage is over $500.

guide.label: Calling the police after a crash
guide.text: At once if anyone is hurt, or damage is over $500.

meta.sourceSection: Section 11, Crashes, under If You Are Involved In A Crash.

content.question: You are in a crash, and the other driver is hurt. What does the law require of you?

choices.text: Stop and give the injured person reasonable help
Call for help, then ride on to find the police
Stay clear, since only trained help may assist
Pull the driver out of the car right away

content.explanation: Stop in a safe place and give reasonable help to anyone injured. Warn approaching traffic if you can do it safely, and exchange names, addresses, plate numbers and license numbers with everyone involved.

guide.text: After a crash, stop somewhere safe, help anyone injured, warn traffic, and swap name, address, plate and license number.

meta.sourceSection: Section 11, Crashes, under If You Are Involved In A Crash.

content.question: You knock the mirror off a parked car, and its owner is nowhere around. What must you do?

choices.text: Find the owner, or leave your name and address for them
Ride on, since nobody was there to see it happen
Ride on, and tell your insurer about it later
Leave a note saying you are sorry, without your details

content.explanation: If you damage an unattended vehicle, find its owner, or leave your name and address and the name of your motorcycle's owner somewhere the owner will find them.

guide.text: Damage an unattended vehicle and you must find the owner or leave your name and address where they will find it.

meta.sourceSection: Section 11, Crashes, under Moving Vehicles Following a Crash.

content.question: A minor crash on a multilane highway leaves no one seriously hurt, and both vehicles can still be driven. What should you do?

choices.text: Move them off the road to a safe place
Leave them in place until the police arrive
Leave them so police can see who was at fault
Move only the vehicle that caused the crash

content.explanation: When no one is seriously hurt and the vehicles can be driven safely, the drivers must move them off a multilane highway to the shoulder, the median or another safe place. Moving them does not make you at fault.

guide.text: Minor crash on a multilane highway, no serious injury: move drivable vehicles off the road. Moving them doesn't make you at fault.

meta.sourceSection: Section 1, Different Types of Vehicles, under Motorcycles.

content.question: In Georgia, what do you need to ride a motorcycle or scooter of more than 50cc on public roads?

choices.text: A Class M license or a Class MP instructional permit
A regular Class C driver's license and nothing more
A Class C license plus a rider course completion card
No license at all, if you stay below 30 mph

content.explanation: Georgia puts motorcycles, scooters and mini-bikes over 50cc in one class. Riding any of them on public roads takes a Class M license or a Class MP instructional permit.

guide.label: License needed to ride
guide.text: A Class M license or Class MP permit, for any motorcycle or scooter over 50cc.

meta.sourceSection: Section 1.1, How to Obtain Your Class M Motorcycle License.

content.question: In Georgia, what are the minimum ages for a Class MP motorcycle permit and a Class M license?

choices.text: 16 for the permit, 17 for the license
15 for the permit, 16 for the license
16 for both the permit and the license
17 for the permit, 18 for the license

content.explanation: Georgia issues a Class MP instructional permit from age 16 and a Class M license from age 17.

guide.label: Minimum ages
guide.text: 16 for a Class MP permit, 17 for a Class M license.

meta.sourceSection: Section 1, General Licensing Information, under Carrying and Displaying Your License.

content.question: Must you have your license or permit with you every time you ride?

choices.text: Yes, and show it to any officer who asks
No, as long as an officer can look it up
No, not for short trips close to home
No, once you hold a full license, not a permit

content.explanation: Carry your license or permit whenever you ride, and show it to any law enforcement officer who asks for it.

meta.sourceSection: Section 3.2, Getting to Know Your Motorcycle; Section 8.1, Carrying Passengers.

content.question: In Georgia, which of these must your motorcycle have before you carry a passenger?

choices.text: Footrests for the passenger
A backrest for the passenger
A second pair of mirrors
Saddlebags for the passenger's gear

content.explanation: Georgia requires passenger footrests on any motorcycle carrying a passenger. The motorcycle should also have a seat big enough for you both, and a strap or handholds the passenger can hold.

guide.text: Carrying a passenger requires passenger footrests. Also have a seat for two and a strap or handholds.

meta.sourceSection: Section 4A.03, meanings of steady signal indications.

content.question: Your light turns green, but a car that entered on the last yellow is still crossing in front of you. What should you do?

choices.text: Wait for it to clear before you go
Go, since the green gives you the right-of-way
Sound your horn and ride around it
Go if it is already past the middle

content.explanation: A green light lets you go, but first yield to pedestrians in the crosswalk and to any vehicle already in the intersection.

guide.label: Steady green light
guide.text: Go, after yielding to pedestrians in the crosswalk and vehicles already in the intersection.

meta.sourceSection: Section 4A.04, meanings of flashing signal indications.

content.question: A flashing yellow arrow pointing left is lit over your left-turn lane. What does it mean?

choices.text: You may turn left after yielding to oncoming traffic
You have a protected turn, so go without stopping
The turn is about to close, so stop now
No left turns until the arrow turns green

content.explanation: A flashing yellow arrow lets you turn, carefully. Yield to oncoming traffic close enough to be a hazard, to pedestrians in the crosswalk, and to vehicles already in the intersection.

guide.label: Flashing yellow arrow
guide.text: Turn with care, after yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians.

meta.sourceSection: Section 4T.02, meaning of lane-use control signal indications.

content.question: On a road with signals mounted over each lane, a steady red X lights up over the lane you are in. What does it mean?

choices.text: The lane is closed to you, so move out of it
The lane is open, but you should slow down
Stop where you are until the X goes out
The lane is for left turns only

content.explanation: A red X means the lane beneath it is closed to traffic going your way. A yellow X warns that the lane is about to close, and a green arrow pointing down means it is open.

guide.label: Signals over lanes
guide.text: Green arrow down: lane open. Yellow X: about to close. Red X: closed.

meta.sourceSection: Section 1.5, Signs, Signals and Road Markings, under the pedestrian beacon panel.

content.question: At a marked crosswalk, an overhead signal's two red lights have been steady and now start flashing in turn. What must you do?

choices.text: Stop, then go once the crosswalk is clear
Stay stopped until the lights go dark
Slow down and go through without stopping
Go at once, since the stop is over

content.explanation: This is a pedestrian hybrid beacon. While both red lights are steady, stay stopped. Once they flash in turn, come to a full stop, then go when pedestrians have cleared the crosswalk.

guide.label: Pedestrian hybrid beacon
guide.text: Steady reds: stop and wait. Reds flashing in turn: stop, then go once the crosswalk is clear.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2C.53, NO PASSING ZONE sign.

content.question: Riding a country road, you see a yellow sign on the left side, shaped like a long triangle pointing right and reading NO PASSING ZONE. What does it mark?

choices.text: Where a no-passing zone begins
Where a no-passing zone ends
Where oncoming traffic may pass you
A passing lane opening on the left

content.explanation: This sign stands on the left side of the road to mark where a no-passing zone begins.

guide.label: No passing zone sign
guide.text: On the left side of the road, where a no-passing zone begins.

meta.sourceSection: Section 1.5, Signs, Signals and Road Markings, crossbuck caption.

content.question: In Georgia, a railroad crossing has a white X-shaped sign reading RAILROAD CROSSING, but no lights or gates. What must you do?

choices.text: Slow down, look and listen, and yield to any train
Stop every time, even with no train in sight
Cross at your usual speed unless you hear a horn
Yield only if a flagger is present

content.explanation: The X-shaped crossbuck marks a railroad crossing. Slow down, look and listen, and yield to any train coming. Where a red light at the crossing is flashing, come to a complete stop.

guide.label: Railroad crossbuck
guide.text: Slow down, look and listen, and yield to any train. A flashing red light means stop.

meta.sourceSection: Section 1.5, crossbuck caption; Section 5.7, under Railroad Crossings.

content.question: You are stopped at a railroad crossing while a train passes. A plaque under the crossing sign reads 2 TRACKS. What should you watch for once the train clears?

choices.text: A second train coming on the other track
The gates staying down a little longer
Traffic behind you trying to go around
Nothing more, since the train has passed

content.explanation: A plaque under the crossbuck gives the number of tracks. Where there is more than one, watch for a second train on another track, from either direction, once the first has passed.

guide.label: Number of tracks plaque
guide.text: More than one railroad track: after one train passes, watch for a second train.

meta.sourceSection: Section 1.5, Signs, Signals and Road Markings, slow-moving vehicle caption.

content.question: In Georgia, the vehicle ahead of you has an orange triangle with a red border on its back. What does that emblem tell you?

choices.text: It moves at less than 25 mph
It moves at less than 45 mph
It is carrying hazardous cargo
It is wider than a normal lane

content.explanation: That emblem marks a slow-moving vehicle, one traveling at less than 25 mph, and Georgia law requires such vehicles to display it.

guide.label: Slow-moving vehicle emblem
guide.text: An orange triangle with a red border: a vehicle moving under 25 mph.

meta.sourceSection: Section 3A.03, marking colors; Section 3B.01, yellow center lines.

content.question: You are riding a road divided down the middle by a single broken yellow line. What does that line tell you?

choices.text: Opposing traffic beyond it; either side may pass with care
Same-way traffic beyond it; you may change lanes with care
Opposing traffic beyond it; neither side may pass
The road splits into separate one-way roads ahead

content.explanation: Yellow center lines separate traffic going in opposite directions, and a single broken yellow line lets traffic on either side pass with care. White lines, by contrast, separate lanes going the same way.

guide.label: Broken yellow center line
guide.text: Oncoming traffic on the other side; passing with care allowed from both sides. White lines separate lanes going the same way.

meta.sourceSection: Section 3B.01, yellow center lines; Figure 3B-1.

content.question: The center line on your road is a double yellow line, solid on your side and broken on the other. May you pass?

choices.text: No, the solid line on your side bars you from passing
Yes, if no traffic is coming the other way
Yes, since the broken line allows passing
Yes, if the vehicle ahead is under the limit

content.explanation: Only traffic next to the broken line may cross the center line to pass. With the solid line on your side you may not, and a double solid yellow line bars passing from both sides.

guide.label: Solid and broken yellow center line
guide.text: Pass only from the broken-line side. Double solid yellow: no passing from either side.

meta.sourceSection: Section 3B.06, white lane lines.

content.question: A double solid white line separates your lane from the next lane going your way. May you move across it?

choices.text: No, a double solid white line bars crossing
Yes, if you signal first and the lane is clear
Yes, since white lines only separate same-way traffic
Yes, if you are moving into a carpool lane

content.explanation: A double solid white line means crossing is prohibited. A single solid white line discourages crossing, and a broken white line lets you change lanes with care.

guide.label: White lane lines
guide.text: Broken: change lanes with care. Single solid: crossing discouraged. Double solid: no crossing.

meta.sourceSection: Section 3A.03, marking colors; Section 3B.09, edge lines.

content.question: On a divided highway, a solid yellow line runs along the left edge of your lane. What does it mark?

choices.text: The left edge of the roadway, with the median beyond
A lane on your left that you may use to pass
Oncoming traffic just on the other side of it
A lane closed for roadwork on your left

content.explanation: On a divided highway or a one-way road, a solid yellow line marks the left edge of the roadway. The right edge is marked in white.

guide.label: Edge lines
guide.text: Yellow on the left edge of a divided or one-way road, white on the right edge.

meta.sourceSection: Section 1.5, Signs, Signals and Road Markings, under Traffic Striping.

content.question: Ahead of a median, the pavement has a triangle of diagonal yellow stripes painted on it. What should you do?

choices.text: Keep to the right of the striped area
Ride across it to pass slower traffic
Wait on it to make a left turn
Stop before it and yield to oncoming traffic

content.explanation: Diagonal yellow stripes mark where the road narrows or an obstruction sits in the roadway. Always keep to the right of them.

guide.text: Diagonal yellow stripes mark a narrowing or an obstruction. Keep to their right.

meta.sourceSection: Section 1.5, Signs, Signals and Road Markings, under Roundabouts.

content.question: You reach a roundabout just as a car already in it comes circling toward your entry point. What should you do?

choices.text: Yield to it, then enter to the right
Enter first, since you are on its right
Enter to the left, against the circle
Sound your horn and enter ahead of it

content.explanation: Traffic already in a roundabout has the right-of-way. Yield to it, enter to the right, and keep circling to the right until you reach your exit.

guide.text: Entering a roundabout, yield to traffic already in it. Enter and circle to the right.

meta.sourceSection: Section 1.1, Class MP Instructional Permit, under MP Restrictions.

content.question: In Georgia, what limits apply while you ride on a Class MP instructional permit?

choices.text: Daylight only, no passengers, and no limited-access highways
Daylight only and no passengers, but any road is open to you
No passengers, but you may ride after dark on any road
Any hour and any road, with a licensed rider following you

content.explanation: On a Georgia Class MP permit you may ride only in daylight, you may not carry a passenger, and you may not use limited-access highways.

guide.label: Class MP permit limits
guide.text: Daylight only, no passengers, no limited-access highways.

meta.sourceSection: Section 3.1, under Helmet Use and Face and Eye Protection.

content.question: What does Georgia law require you to wear when you ride?

choices.text: A DOT-compliant helmet and eye protection
A DOT-compliant helmet, with eye protection left up to you
Eye protection, plus a helmet only if you are under 21
A helmet and eye protection, unless the bike has a windshield

content.explanation: Georgia law requires a DOT-compliant helmet, one meeting the U.S. Department of Transportation standard, along with eye protection.

meta.sourceSection: Section 3.2, Getting to Know Your Motorcycle.

content.question: In Georgia, how high above the seat may your motorcycle's handlebars be?

choices.text: No more than 25 inches
No more than 15 inches
No more than 30 inches
No more than 36 inches

content.explanation: Georgia law limits handlebar height to 25 inches above the rider's seat.

guide.label: Handlebar height
guide.text: No more than 25 inches above the seat.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2.3, Emotions.

content.question: You are about to ride while still angry after an argument. How can strong emotions affect your riding?

choices.text: They can distract you and make you more willing to take risks
Anger can sharpen your attention, at least on a short ride
They matter little once you are an experienced rider
They only matter when you are also tired or have been drinking

content.explanation: Strong feelings such as anger, fear or worry pull your attention off the road, slow how quickly you take in what is happening, and make risks seem more acceptable.

guide.text: Strong emotions such as anger, fear or worry can distract you and lead you to take more risks.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2.1, under Don't Drink or Don't Ride.

content.question: You have had a few drinks and want to sober up before riding home. What actually works?

choices.text: Waiting, since nothing else speeds it up
A cup of strong coffee before you leave
A brisk walk to work it out of your system
A cold shower to clear your head

content.explanation: Only time sobers you up. Coffee, a cold shower or exercise will not make it happen any faster.

meta.sourceSection: Section 4.2, Riding in a Straight Line, under Friction Zone.

content.question: What is a motorcycle clutch's friction zone?

choices.text: The point where engine power starts reaching the rear wheel
The point where the clutch lever is fully released
The throttle range where the rear tire may lose grip
The part of the brake lever's travel where braking begins

content.explanation: As you ease out the clutch lever, the friction zone is where the engine's power first starts to reach the rear wheel. Add throttle there to pull away, and let the lever out the rest of the way once the motorcycle is moving steadily.

guide.label: Friction zone
guide.text: Where the clutch first starts sending engine power to the rear wheel.

meta.sourceSection: Section 4.3, Shifting Gears, under Starting on an Incline.

content.question: You are stopped facing uphill and about to pull away. Which brake should hold the motorcycle while your right hand works the throttle?

choices.text: The rear brake, held with your foot
The front brake, held with two fingers as you twist
Neither, since the clutch can hold it on its own
Both, released together as soon as you are in gear

content.explanation: Keep the front brake on as you start up and click into first, then move to the rear brake so your right hand is free for the throttle. Let the rear brake go once the engine speed dips, the sign that the clutch has started to pull.

guide.text: Uphill starts: front brake on to start up and select first, then rear brake on while you add throttle and ease out the clutch.

meta.sourceSection: Section 4.1, Getting Started, under Starting the Engine.

content.question: Before starting the engine, how can you be sure the motorcycle is in neutral?

choices.text: Rock it with the clutch out and see that it moves easily
Check that the neutral indicator light is lit
Squeeze the clutch lever and see whether it rolls
Press the shift lever down until it will go no further

content.explanation: The neutral light can be wrong, so check by feel: leave the clutch lever out and rock the motorcycle a little. It is in neutral only if it moves easily.

meta.sourceSection: Ride Within Your Abilities, under Turning.

content.question: You are approaching a turn. When and how should you reduce your speed?

choices.text: Before the turn, by easing off the throttle and braking if needed
Once you are in the turn and can see clearly where it leads
Before the turn, by shifting into neutral and coasting into it
Halfway through, once the motorcycle has settled into its lean

content.explanation: Do your slowing before the turn, not in it. Roll off the throttle, and add both brakes if that alone is not enough.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5.3, Intersections, under Traffic-Activated Sensor Lights.

content.question: The traffic light at an intersection ahead changes only when a sensor detects a waiting vehicle. Where should you stop your motorcycle?

choices.text: Directly over the sensor, which usually shows in the pavement
Anywhere in the lane, since the sensor picks up any vehicle
Far enough back that a car can stop over the sensor instead
At the edge of the lane, in clear view of the signal head

content.explanation: Sensors that trigger a signal may miss a motorcycle, so stop right where the sensor is. You can usually spot it in the pavement.

meta.sourceSection: Section 7.1, Crowned Roads.

content.question: On a crowned road, one that is higher in the middle than at the edges, which curves call for extra care, and why?

choices.text: Curves to the left, with less ground clearance and lean available
Curves to the right, because the slope pushes you toward the edge
Curves either way, because a crowned surface is more slippery
Neither, since the crown only helps rain drain off the road

content.explanation: A crowned road slopes down from the middle toward each edge. In a curve to the left, that slope cuts your ground clearance and leaves you less lean to work with than on a flat road.

guide.text: On a crowned road, take left-hand curves with care: the slope leaves less ground clearance and lean.

meta.sourceSection: Section 7.2, Work Zones.

content.question: A work zone ahead has sand and gravel scattered across the pavement. How should you brake through it?

choices.text: Lightly, with the motorcycle upright and traveling straight
Firmly, using the rear brake alone so the front cannot slide
Hard on the front, since it holds most of your stopping power
Not at all; shift to neutral and coast across it

content.explanation: Take sand and gravel slowly and smoothly, with no sudden turns. Brake gently and only while upright and going straight; across a long stretch, drop a gear and hold your speed steady.

guide.text: Work-zone sand or gravel: slow down, brake gently and only while upright and straight, and on a long stretch downshift and hold a steady speed.

meta.sourceSection: Section 7.2, Work Zones.

content.question: You are riding over scored, grooved pavement in a work zone, and the motorcycle feels unsettled. What should you do?

choices.text: Look well ahead, hold the throttle steady and don't fight the bars
Look down at the grooves so you can steer a path between them
Grip the bars hard and steer against the wandering feeling
Speed up a little so the tires skim across the tops of the grooves

content.explanation: Look up and well ahead rather than down at the grooves, keep your speed down and the throttle even, and let the motorcycle move a little under you instead of wrestling the handlebars.

guide.text: On grooved work-zone pavement, look up, keep it slow with an even throttle, and let the bars move instead of wrestling them.

meta.sourceSection: Section 7.2, Work Zones.

content.question: In a work zone, the lane beside you has been repaved and sits higher than yours. How should you cross the edge to move into it?

choices.text: Slowly, and at a sharper angle rather than a shallow drift
Quickly, so you spend as little time as possible on the edge
Gradually, easing across it at a long, shallow angle
At your normal speed, once you have signaled the change

content.explanation: The step between a repaved lane and one still waiting for paving can make you lose control if you cross it fast or at a narrow angle. Slow down, and cross it at a wider angle.

guide.text: Crossing a raised lane edge in a work zone, slow down and avoid a shallow angle; fast and narrow can cost you control.

meta.sourceSection: Section 7.5, Wind.

content.question: A strong gust of wind is pushing you from the right. How do you counter it?

choices.text: Press forward on the right grip, leaning into the wind
Press forward on the left grip, steering away from the wind
Lean your body left while holding the bars straight
Brake firmly and hold your line until the gust passes

content.explanation: Counter a gust by leaning into it: press forward on the handgrip on the side the wind is coming from. Also move away from passing vehicles, keep plenty of space around you, and park somewhere safe if the wind gets too strong.

guide.text: In a gust, lean into the wind by pressing forward on the handgrip on the side it comes from. Park if it gets too strong.

meta.sourceSection: Section 9.1, Cold Weather.

content.question: You are riding on a cold day. Besides dressing warmly, how should you adjust your riding?

choices.text: Ride slower and leave more space ahead and beside you
Ride a little faster so you spend less time in the cold
Follow closer behind larger vehicles to stay out of the wind
Nothing changes, as long as your gear keeps you warm

content.explanation: Cold slows your reactions. Make up for it by riding slower and leaving more room ahead of you and to each side.

meta.sourceSection: Section 2.1, under Other Impairing Drugs and Riding.

content.question: Which drugs can affect your ability to ride safely?

choices.text: Prescription, over-the-counter and illegal drugs alike
Only illegal drugs, since legal medicines are tested for safety
Only prescription drugs that carry a drowsiness warning
Only drugs taken together with alcohol

content.explanation: Any drug can affect your riding, whether a doctor prescribed it, you bought it over the counter, or it is illegal. If you are unsure about one, ask your doctor or pharmacist, and never mix it with alcohol, which it can make stronger.

guide.text: Prescription, over-the-counter and illegal drugs can all affect your riding. Never mix them with alcohol.

meta.sourceSection: Section 3.2, Getting to Know Your Motorcycle.

content.question: When should you set your mirrors, and what should they give you?

choices.text: Before you ride, set for the best view of the road behind
Once moving, when you can see how traffic is lined up behind
Only after a stop, when you notice a mirror has slipped
Before you ride, tilted down to show your rear wheel

content.explanation: Setting the mirrors is part of getting your motorcycle ready before you ride. Aim them for the best view of the road behind you.

meta.sourceSection: Section 3.3, Motorcycle Controls.

content.question: How well should you know your motorcycle's controls before you ride it?

choices.text: Well enough to work them while riding, without looking for them
Well enough to find each one with a quick glance down
The brakes and throttle only; the rest can wait until later
Well enough to name each one; using them comes with practice

content.explanation: Learn from the owner's manual where every control is and how it works, until you can operate each one on the move without hunting for it.

guide.text: Know your controls well enough to work them while riding without looking; the owner's manual shows where they are.

meta.sourceSection: Section 4.3, Shifting Gears.

content.question: You want to change down to a lower gear. What do you do with the shift lever?

choices.text: Press it down firmly, without stomping on it
Lift it firmly, then let it spring back
Stamp down hard, so the gear is sure to engage
Press it down and keep holding it until you speed up

content.explanation: With the throttle closed and the clutch in, push the shift lever down with firm pressure, no stomping, then let it go. Shifting up is the reverse: you lift the lever.

guide.text: Press the shift lever down to change down and lift it to change up, firmly but without stomping.

meta.sourceSection: Section 5.4, Space Management, under Lane Positions.

content.question: Big patches of oil and grease are a hazard to a motorcycle. Where do they usually build up?

choices.text: At busy intersections and toll booths
On the shoulders of rural highways
In the passing lane of an interstate
On bridge decks and overpasses

content.explanation: Heavy oil and grease usually collect at busy intersections and toll booths, so steer around those patches rather than riding through them.

meta.sourceSection: Section 6.1, Crash Avoidance, under Stopping Quickly.

content.question: You need to stop as quickly as you can in a straight line. How should you brake?

choices.text: Both brakes at once, firm but short of locking either wheel
The front brake alone, squeezed as hard as it will go
The rear brake first, then the front once you have slowed
Both brakes at full pressure from the very first instant

content.explanation: The quickest stop uses both brakes at the same time, pressed hard but never to the point where a wheel locks.

meta.sourceSection: Section 6.1, Crash Avoidance, under Stopping Quickly.

content.question: During a quick stop, how should the pressure on your front brake change?

choices.text: Build it gradually as the motorcycle's weight shifts forward
Start at full pressure, then ease off as you slow
Keep it steady from the first moment to the last
Ease it off as weight shifts forward, so the rear does more

content.explanation: As you brake, the motorcycle's weight moves forward onto the front tire, so increase front brake pressure gradually as the stop goes on instead of applying it all at the start.

guide.text: In a quick stop, build front brake pressure gradually as weight shifts onto the front tire.

meta.sourceSection: Section 6.1, Crash Avoidance, under Stopping Quickly.

content.question: During a quick stop, what posture helps keep the motorcycle stopping in a straight line?

choices.text: Knees pressed to the tank, eyes up and looking well ahead
Knees off the tank, eyes down on the front wheel
Leaning back with your arms locked straight
Knees relaxed, eyes on the pavement just ahead
